This run covered 21 EKS-health evals (123 iterations, no failures, no cleanup issues). One eval ("eks-health-smoke-test") was a should_trigger:false check and all its downstream dimensions were correctly skipped, not a weak result. The trigger itself fired 100% of the time for both variants across every eval, so the behavior-under-test consistently activated.

The dominant and highly consistent pattern across nearly every eval with real assertion data is that with_skill met the "expected output" criterion at or near 100% (high confidence) while without_skill scored 0% (or very low, e.g. 17–33%) on the same expected-output checks. This gap is not a single metric artifact — it shows up at the per-assertion level too: in eval after eval, specific assertions (e.g. naming correct health domains, stating the skill is read-only, correct CP source-fallback order, N/A-grading rules, FP-guard identification, dashboard section naming) are "with_skill_passes_without_skill_fails," often 3/3 vs 0/3 with high confidence on both sides. A smaller number of assertions were "always_fails" for both variants (e.g. "states this skill is read-only" dashboard phrasing nuances, "same-day artifact refreshed not duplicated," and one domain-naming nuance in "three-domains") — these indicate the assertion or underlying behavior needs work regardless of variant, not a variant weakness. A few assertions were "always_passes" for both (e.g. memory-leak-alone caveat, declining to recommend control-plane scaling) — these don't differentiate the variants. Some assertions were flaky (partial pass rates like 1/3 or 2/3) for one or both variants, signaling run-to-run variability in grading or behavior rather than a clean pass/fail.

In a couple of evals (e.g. "eks-health-read-only-contract," "eks-health-cluster-confirmation-gate," "eks-health-source-detection-gap" for scenario-based ones), without_skill's assertion/expected-output data is marked null or "inconclusive," meaning no verdict could be reached for that variant — this is an absence of data, not evidence of poor performance.

On runtime and cost, with_skill was consistently faster and cheaper than without_skill across almost every eval where both ran (e.g. 7s/$0.06 vs 38s/$0.32, 4s/$0.04 vs 29s/$0.25, 12s/$0.10 vs 1m13s/$0.61), sometimes by a large margin (up to ~5-10x). In a couple of evals runtimes were close (e.g. "eks-health-source-detection-gap": 4s vs 7s; "eks-health-scenario-confidence-contract": 8s vs 8s) or even without_skill nominally lower (one 0s case, likely a skipped/degenerate run). Context-window utilization was low and similar for both (~4–5.6%) with no compaction events, indicating headroom was not a differentiator.

Output consistency (run-to-run stability) was measured on a 1–3 scale ("consistent" to "inconsistent"). Variant_b landed mostly in the "consistent" to "mostly_consistent" range (scores 2.0–3.0, mostly high confidence) across nearly all evals. Variant_a's consistency varied more: some evals show "consistent" or "mostly_consistent" (comparable to with_skill), but others show lower scores, including one "inconsistent" (1.67) in "eks-health-scenario-findings-no-invented-thresholds," and several null values where consistency could not be computed (often tied to the missing/inconclusive assertion data above). This suggests without_skill's output stability is more mixed and, in some cases, simply unmeasured.

Direct quality comparison (pairwise LLM judging of output quality) was mostly skipped — in the large majority of evals, "pairs_evaluated" was 0 and 3 pairs were skipped, so no head-to-head quality verdict exists for those evals. Only three evals had quality comparisons: "eks-health-scenario-429-workload-low-informational" (without_skill favored 7 times vs with_skill favored 1, across accuracy/completeness/actionability, medium confidence), "eks-health-scenario-empty-query-not-pass" (with_skill favored 2 vs without_skill 0, medium confidence, only 1 of 3 pairs evaluated), and no quality data for the rest. These are sparse, low-pair-count samples and should be read as weak, partial signals rather than a definitive quality verdict — notably the one eval with the strongest quality signal in without_skill's favor ("429-workload") is also one where without_skill's expected-output match was good (3/3) but its per-assertion pass rate was still only 50%, showing the dimensions don't all point the same direction even within a single eval.

Overall, the pattern across this suite is that with_skill met the specific expected-output and assertion criteria far more often (frequently 100% vs 0%, high confidence) and ran faster/cheaper in most evals, while without_skill showed more variable consistency and, in the two evals with direct quality judging, mixed results (favored in one, not in the other, both based on very few judged pairs). Several assertions and one full eval were skipped or inconclusive for structural reasons (should_trigger:false, missing data for without_skill), and a handful of assertions failed for both variants or passed for both, meaning they don't discriminate between the variants and point instead to shared gaps or shared strengths in the underlying skill behavior.
